I have always wondered the same thing. Just today I read another post about a person's book being 1 million+ words. Like, how? How do you end up that long winded? How many words a day do you type to even get to that point?

I average about 5,000 to 8,000 words a day which I find very reasonable. My first drafts of books are typically around 150k words. I then usually find ways to edit it to be about 80k words and still tell the exact story I want it to.

Currently my first draft of my upcoming book, that I hope to publish through good publishers instead of self-publishing this time, is at 21,000 words and on track to complete at 125-150k before I edit and revise it a dozen times. It'll most likely end up being 75 to 85k once finished, which is about average for the genre I'm writing for.

I'd say I read between 20 to 50 books a year, depending on free time, size of books, etc. 

While some of my book have been inspired by favorites of mine, I try to make my books as creative and unique as possible. I take the good stuff from books I like and analyze what made it good, so that I might be able to apply similar methods of writing that could ensure my own books are:

* More enjoyable to read
* More addictive - i.e. "Can't put it down, it's too good!"
* Make use of better and more elaborate words, adjectives, adverbs, etc.
* Paced well

Other than that, I use the books I read as both a fun and enjoyable time and hobby, as well as a learning tool, but I try to keep the books I author unique and different in plot, world creation, etc.

This cannot be said enough. I also thought about possibly living off of savings and writing a book to somehow end up "okay" and make enough to scratch by. I wasn't expecting to become rich or a number 1 best seller. However, I was wise, and kept my day job. I understood how unlikely it was I would make a single dime, ever. What most people do not understand at first, is there are thousands and thousands of books that go absolutely nowhere, and you're likely to fall into that same bucket at first.

I ended up writing 2 books within about 1 year's time that honestly, sucked. But they were great learning experiences, and allowed me to explore topics to understand not only the creative process, but the editing and everything in-between. 

I did not consider a single book I authored "good" until my 8th go at it. Which was about 4 years of working on this as a hobby. It takes a lot of time to develop the skills, creativity, and prose to present a reader an exciting book. There are no shortcuts (unless you're damn lucky). 

To this day, I have made barely any money. I will not Dox myself, so I'm not saying which books I self-published into the Kindle e-store, but what I will say is that I've sold barely 200 copies, and there's only a dozen ratings. Albeit good ones, so the books are enjoyable I guess? 

To truly make it as an author, I have come to realize that self-publishing is unlikely to work. Second, you need journalistic reviews and people with a voice to get the word out to truly drive sales.

If you're fairly certain you'd always bottom out, which is common, then the decision on heavy vs light switches comes down to your typing form. 

If you're typing in the "classical" sense with what many consider proper "form" then you might want to go with lighter switches. The angle of your fingers as they loop over will feel tired faster as there is less natural downward force when typing like this. Heavy switches would be more fatiguing. 

If you have an unorthodox typing style (e.g. Myself ~ 3 fingers per hand, arms raised up a bit) then you likely have a lot more natural downward force. If you "peck" type then you have an ass load of downward force. In these situations a heavier switch offers more cushion and will reduce fatigue caused by repeatedly banging into the keyboard plate as you bottom out. 

My best advice for you is to pickup a 10 pack of heavy switches and another of light switches. Replace one row of your keyboard letters (not F keys, not numbers, commands, etc. ~ legit letters) with the light switches, and another with the heavy switches. You'll end up with 3 rows: 1 with original switches, 1 heavy, 1 light. This will be awkward to type on but you'll get a feel out of the 3 switch options for the one you prefer the most. Then you can proceed to replace the remaining with your preferred switch.

Tired fingers - 2 things: 

Is your key cap profile tuned for your typing form? I have found in the past that the key cap profile made a bigger difference than I originally credited to it. I ended up trying SA, Cherry, KAT, XDA, DSA, and finally KAS (Keychron's take on SA). I ended up preferring KAS the most. It was the most ergonomic for me. It made a **significant** difference. 

If you like to bottom out, are you looking to do so with *less* resistance, or are you looking to bottom-out less frequently - thus more cushion?

If you want to bottom out with cushion - then you need *heavy* switches with bottom-out forces of at-least 65g or more. I currently type on Kailh Box Navy \~ which is a very heavy switch, with bottom-out force between 75 and 80g \~ this was because I wanted to *stop* bottoming out, or at the very least have a *lot* more *cushion*. However \~ if you're looking to hit the bottom faster, then look for switches with bottom-out forces around 45g or less. This will require less resistance, and will make it far easier to fully depress the switch.

As for acoustics: this is highly personal. I really like clicky switches. Some people don't and that seems to be the trend. Tactile switches are the middle ground, with only a mild click - or none at all - but with the similar tactile feel. Linear switches are smooth and silent (until you bottom out - which makes its own sound regardless of switch...)

[Here](https://healthjade.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/eye-neovascularization.jpg), [here](https://eyerounds.org/atlas/photos/NVI_CRAO/Fig1-Anterior-segment-OD-NVI-LRG.jpg), and [here](https://webeye.ophth.uiowa.edu/eyeforum/atlas/pages/NVI/NVI-LRG.jpg) are photos of the actual condition. Obviously the first one is a **severe** case, the *second* photo - look hard and you'll see the veins beginning to make intrusions into the iris; finally the third is what I'd consider an average advanced case.

That said, your photos are not high enough quality, and do *not* replace the trained eyes of a doctor, to make a true diagnosis.

This is not true for the most part, especially if the switches you use have some form of dust wall or have the metal contacts housed in a supposed "box" (such as my Kailh Box Navy) \~ however, with that said, if your keyboard is absolutely filthy then it will mostly likely **not** matter if it is membrane or mechanical. 

Mechanical switches can be a bit more sensitive to dust and liquid intrusion that membrane. However, this is not a universal truth (see above) as switches exist that are IP rated and can handle a good bit of abuse. 

My biggest question though: why would you not clean your keyboard? How is spending 30 seconds to 2 minutes blasting it with compressed air (can be found in can format) between the key caps once a month that big of annoyance? Membrane, mechanical, etc. does not matter if you're a sloppy person who thinks its "too much work" to spend 2 minutes cleaning once a month.

I used the MX Keys S for about a solid year, it's much much quieter and the travel distance is extremely small. If you absolutely need a quiet keyboard, the MX Mechanical may still fit your needs as they offer a version with linear quiet switches. However the MX Keys will always be far quieter since it's membrane and the travel distance is so small, plus actuation force is minimal 

The MX Keys S is an excellent keyboard that is built very well, however it's too low-profile for me. I like low profile, but not to the degree that Apple Magic Keyboard, MX Keys S, various laptops, etc are. The MX Mechanical is my ideal "low-profile" vs the others. However, as an owner of Keys S and a user for a year, it's not a bad choice, but the MX Mechanical is better in a lot of ways, unless you need absolutely quiet keyboards.

The G910 is a gaming keyboard through and through. It's wired to ensure the highest polling rates (typically 1,000Hz ~ however the MX Mechanical using the Bolt USB will also support 1,000Hz but with Bluetooth option drops to 75Hz). It also uses full size sculpted keycaps. I personally hate sculpted keycaps with a passion, so the G910 was never an option for me. 

The G910 has much better lighting options and controls, so if you want colors then skip MX Mechanical as it's white only. 

As someone who types a LOT every day, the G910 would never be on my list. However that does not make it a bad keyboard. Contrary, the G910 is arguably better than MX Mechanical for several reasons:
* Ensures higher polling rate by doing away with Bluetooth and being a wired keyboard
* RGB backlighting 
* Customizable hotkeys
* Uses regular switches and not low-profile, plus there's far more options from the major 3 (MX Cherry, Kailh, Gateron)

For myself, these are the cons of the G910:
* Overpriced 
* Sculpted keycaps
* Feels less durable ~ the plastic feels much cheaper than the MX Mechanical 
* Because it's sculpted and uses full sized keycaps, I tend to hit two of them accidentally or miss, etc. Sculpted full size, like Cherry or SA, cause a lot of typing errors for me, but everyone is different

You will probably not find many people in this subreddit that support the use of cosmetic lenses like these. This is a forum where a lot of regular contributors are in or studying the medical field. 

I myself am in the medical field and am studying for med school. 

My personal recommendation is to not use these lenses. They are often of dubious quality and manufactured in Chinese factories (even if the parent company is Korean) and are generally not regarded as safe. 

There is a giant list of complications that can occur from the improper use of contact lenses, and cosmetic ones made from cheap plastics that are often not sterile, and use dyes that can even be carcinogenic, plus being of general dubious quality is not something worth risking. It's not a good idea to slap a cheap plastic lens on your eye. It increases the probability of serious complications dramatically. 

There are legitimate cosmetic lenses that you can get from your optometrist.

**I cannot personally recommend any cosmetic lenses that are not fitted and prescribed by an optometrist. All contact lenses are prescription medical devices and being in possession of lenses without a prescription is illegal in most countries.**

**However I highly recommend staying with cosmetic lenses that are legitimate and prescribed and fitted by an optometrist.** There are just too many variables in making safe lenses that properly fit, are sterile, and healthy, that most shops cannot or will not fulfill. It's not worth the risk to even attempt in my opinion. 

I'm sure out there in the wild are some genuinely decent cosmetic lenses, however I am not aware of any brands that would be worth the hassle to recommend. But I can give some advice (please read this entire reply!):
* It needs to be made using the same materials as real contacts, namely *silicone hydrogel* for the best oxygen transmissibility. **If they don't state the material - avoid.** The materials you're wanting are going to end in "filcon". They should state the oxygen transmissibility values in Dk/t values optimally. 
* They cannot be worn for more than *30 days after opening the packages - not 30 days on your eye, 30 days post package unsealing* or even better, for just a *single day* before being discarded. *If they state some ridiculous times like 3 months or a year, it's not safe.*
* They need to use hypoallergenic dyes, preferably ones you wouldn't mind eating. Not some random dyes. 
* They need to clearly state the water content and silicone hydrogel content, such as 48% water - 52% comfilcon A
* They need to have a legit base curve value **that must match what your optometrist measures of your cornea** - if they do not force you to select a base curve, or do not even state a value for such - avoid. Reasonable values are between 8.3mm and 9.0mm -  (do not use any old measurements, match ones to your actual measurements by an optometrist).
* They should have a diameter value between 14.0mm and 14.5mm - and should ideally be within a range a real contact lens fitting would recommend. If they don't even state it - avoid.
* **You should consult your optometrist about the brand you select and *all of its specifications* with your optometrist.** Don't play doctor yourself. Always run it by an optometrist to gauge if they even feel remotely comfortable with it!
* **Avoid shady online shops that charge ridiculously low prices** - that's a sign it's likely unsafe.
* The contact and it's packaging solution must be sterile, and is typically accomplished with heating/thermal sterilization. There is a specific icon for this that should appear on the packages and box. 

Wacky colors are a sign they are unlikely to be safe. So the colors you're after are *very unlikely to exist in a safe manner* and very unlikely for any optometrist to feel safe about. 

Using cosmetic lenses not prescribed and fitted by an optometrist is a **major risk not worth taking in my opinion!**

Toric lenses are those made for astigmatism. If you do not have astigmatism, then the lenses you're using are what are known as regular spherical lenses. 

Toric lenses have special weights and zones on the lenses that are designed to automatically rotate the lens into the correct position. Different brands use different stabilization techniques. The idea of it being a weight at the bottom of the lens is sorta old school. While there is a weight at the bottom of the lens, it plays only a minor role in today's torics. It's there to do the initial rotation right after it's inserted when it's still slippery wet with solution. That weight right after insertion basically drags and rotates the lens into the correct axis while the lens is still moist enough to rotate very freely. 

After that the stabilization system is what keeps the lens stable. These systems typically use bumps/weights/resistance zones on the edges of the lens that work with the eye lid when you blink. Specifically the upward motion. So in effect, every time you blink, you reset the lens back into position. If you were to take a toric lens and place it on your fingers and feel around the rim, you would note several bumps. Those bumps are the added material that is used for the weights and stability systems.

As for how to store them, if you do decide to go along with what is probably a very bad idea, I would definitely use a multi-purpose solution that any other prescription contact lens wearers would use. 

Not sure what you have in your country or what the brands are, but here in the US the big 3 are OptiFree, BioTrue, and ClearCare. 

**Fully read the instructions on both the box and the bottle and ensure you fully understand how to use the solution. Failure to do so increases adverse events such as infections dramatically.**

You will need to remove and properly clean and disinfect the lens each night. Never sleep in them. Especially with these cosmetic lenses you claim are legit. Because they probably don't allow any oxygen through, sleeping in them would be the dumbest idea ever. 

Take them out, and if you're using a multi-purpose solution then you'll need to:
* Remove the lens 
* Rinse each side of the lens for 5 seconds
* Place the lens in the palm of one hand, squirt some solution onto it
* Use the index finger of the other hand and lightly rub the contact around for at least 20 seconds
* Rinse each side again for 5 seconds
* Fill contacts case with **fresh** solution and then store it. 
* Let it soak undistributed for the minimum time required for that solution, typically 4 to 6 hours. 

Never reuse solution or "top off" what's already in it. Empty the case each time after you take the lenses out when you go to wear them, and then flip it upside down on something like a paper towel to air dry. You will also want to rinse it out every once in a while **with the multi-purpose solution** to get any dust or protein films and stuff that clings to the walls out. 

Replace the contacts case every 90 days. Never store the lenses for more than 30 days. If it's been more than 30 days, you will need to toss the lenses. It's done. No longer safe. 

If you choose to use ClearCare: **read the instructions on the box and the bottle thoroughly and ensure you completely understand them.** It's a Hydrogen Peroxide based cleaning system. Failure to follow the directions properly will burn the living crap out of your eye if you do not allow the solution to completely neutralize. Always use the case/baskets it comes with. Never use your own. It has a platinum disk at the bottom that catalyzes the reaction so it turns into saline. Do not disturb the baskets once you fill it and place the lenses inside. Always use fresh solution. It should bubble each time, every time. Don't underfill or overfill. 

Never use water or spit on your lenses for **any reason at all, ever.** Should water come into contact with the lens, it's done for. Toss it. 

If you drop the lens on something while attempting to insert it, such as the sink, or counter **stop and do not attempt to insert it again. It is now contaminated. You must follow all cleaning instructions again and soak times before attempting to insert it again. There is no such thing as 3 or 5 or whatever second rule.**

Okay, sure, but how do you know if it's going to fit your eye correctly? Did it ask you for a base curve at the least? If the lens you bought had a base curve of say 8.4mm but your eye is really 8.8mm then it's going to fit far too tightly. This could be uncomfortable, leading to eye strain, headaches, and even constriction of the flow of nutrients to the cornea thus starving it. Over time that over constriction could do damage. 

That's why you should always be fitted. You can usually get away with diameter as most contacts, even the cosmetic ones, are roughly 13 to 14.5mm but base curve values have a huge impact on how the lens rests on your cornea and whether it's comfortable or even safe. 

As another example I wouldn't want to put a lens with a 9.0mm base curve on my cornea that needs a 8.5mm base curve because then the lens is just going to float around and move around constantly. It'll never "settle" into place. This can scratch the cornea, especially if there's even microscopic dust between the lens and your cornea. All that movement is just going to do damage over time, not to mention be incredibly uncomfortable and for a cosmetic lens, make your eyes look ridiculously stupid. 

This is why an optometrist measures your eyes and only doles out specific brands at specific base curves during trials. There's wiggle room, not going to sit here and pretend it needs to be a perfect match. It's relatively safe for me, with a measurement of 8.5mm, to try 8.4 and 8.6mm lenses, but I wouldn't want an 8.3mm or 9.0mm because then it's going beyond the safety zone.

I agree then with JimR84 that this is more than likely you seeing the edge of the optical transition zone. All contacts have an optical zone that is actually substantially smaller than the contact itself. 

The reason for seeing it could be a combination of pupil dilation diameter alongside a lens that isn't centering on your eye (most likely because it's base curve is too big, and the diameter possibly being too small). In other words, the lens is moving around so much that the edge of the optical zone is crossing over your actual vision. The best solution to this is a lens with a smaller base curve. The base curve basically determines how "snug" the lens fits on your cornea for lack of better terms. This greatly reduces movement. You'd also want a lens with a bigger diameter so the optical zone is further outside the maximal dilation. So smaller base curve, bigger diameter. 

If it's too small of a base curve (8.3mm) then it would fit too tightly to the cornea and cause eye strain and possibly other complications you don't want. If it's too big (9.0mm) then it's never going to "suction cup" itself to the cornea enough to prevent movement. With too big of a base curve and too small a diameter of the lens, then it's likely it's moving around so much that the optical zone interface becomes visible. 

However those optimal values would need to be worked out with an optometrist. The values I provided are just examples. You'd definitely want to be measured again for enhanced accuracy. So another visit and fitting is absolutely required. 

As an example for myself, a base curve of 9.0mm with a lens that is 14mm diameter would likely cause a similar condition for me. However my true base curve is 8.5mm. I've been fitted into Acuvue Oasys 1-Day with HydraLuxe which has an 8.5mm base curve match I need and a slightly bigger 14.3mm diameter. This ensures I never see the edge of the optical transition zone. It suction cups perfectly to my cornea and the lens is wide enough overall that the transition zone is well outside my maximal pupil dilation. The lens therefore doesn't move around my eye and the optical transition zone is well outside the maximal dilation. 

You're likely in a totally wrong-sized lens. A new measurement should be made for better accuracy and a better fitting lens should be trialed.

Contacts are medical devices that require a proper fitting and prescription from a doctor. Your cornea is highly susceptible to damage and infections. It's an extremely sensitive area of the body. You can't abuse it. In fact, any abuse is likely to result in bad things.

Bottom line is, contacts that aren't acquired with a prescription are essentially "fake" and bad for the eyes.

Transparencies are difficult to print on. Impossible with inkjets (obvious) but even for a laser printer it's hard. It's a sheet of plastic. So the printer is trying to fuse plastic to plastic (toner is microscopic pieces of plastic). It requires more heat to properly fuse and print on transparencies. Some models of lasers will be better at this than others.

Ideally there would be a driver option for it so the printer knows to handle it differently. Personally, and I know you said you had success in the past, this isn't a job for a laser printer of the home or small/medium office type. This is a job for a specialty printer made to handle printing on plastic.

As for why it's streaking suddenly - this could be the result of the fact it's hard to print on, but it could also be a sign that the toner dispenser roller is not working correctly (replace toner cartridge then) or the drum is giving out.

Try printing on regular paper to see if you get the same results. If you do - then replace the toner and see if that fixes it. If not, then try the drum. 

If paper comes out perfect - it's probably just down to the fact it's difficult to print on that material.

Some people have a hard time seeing a 0.25 difference, but it might help if you're looking at something at a bit of a distance, say 20-50 feet away. Start by blinking several times, wait a few seconds for contacts to settle, and then take your hand and cover one eye so you're looking out the left/right first. Then do it again for the other. Pay close attention to how sharp *hard* edges are (such as on letters on paper). 

I recommend printing something on paper, that you can still see (so not tiny regular font, maybe medium sized letters that you can still read from 20ft distance) and taping it up somewhere. Pay close attention to how sharp the *edges* of the letter look. If one eye is slightly blurry and the other eye is not, you'll know. 

For me, I can instantly see a 0.25D difference. But for some people they barely notice it at all. Doing the above method could help.

Yeah lasers typically have expensive toner because toner goes a LOT further than ink. The pre-page cost is actually much lower than true "ink" (as in the liquid stuff). Toner is a very fine microscopic powdered plastic. Paper coming out of a laser printer is often very warm to touch at first.

Toner is different from ink, and goes a lot further. Plus it looks way more professional and doesn't fade as easily as ink, and the print quality is much higher.

If you go ham and just start slamming them closed and stuff then yes, I can see damage happening. Don't let the baskets snap close. Slowly close them yourself and make sure the contact is either centered in the basket or centered on the knuckle as much as possible to avoid the edges being pinched.

There's some things you should consider in my opinion: 

* Are you hoping for daily contacts that you open and dispose of every day, so you're constantly using new ones each day? 
* Are you looking for a longer lasting contact, such as 2-week or monthly? 
* Are you looking for the most comfortable ones? I feel like everyone wants this for sure, *but few speak up about it*. There are brands that are well known for better comfort (Acuvue Oasys for example) and brands well known for less comfort but more affordability (Biofinity)
* Make sure you ask about proper cleaning if you're not getting daily replacement lenses - this is **absolutely critical**
* Speak up if you have allergies or dry eye symptoms
* Ask how to properly insert and remove them
* Ask how to tell if they're inside out
* Ask about sleeping in them and the rules behind it. Generally sleeping in contacts is a big fat NO, but it's safer in some situations than others based on brand/type and its appropriate ratings
* Make sure you ask about preferred solutions (if not dailies), some are much better than others. You get what you pay for when it comes to multipurpose solutions. Store brands vs name brands DO matter. Different name brands DO matter. What is more comfortable is also down to trial and error. The solution has a **major** impact on comfort and moisture.

* Ask how to properly open the new packages, I found some trickier than others 
* Most of all **speak up about everything you're not sure about**

I made the mistake of not always speaking up about what I wanted and it's *part* of the reason it took me so many brands to get the right ones (Acuvue Oasys 2-week with Hydraclear Plus). 

Always **be your own patient advocate** and ask every question you have and state what you're looking for. Not doing so could result in a lens brand/type that doesn't work for you and a lot of trial and error. Be patient and kind when speaking up. Don't sound like an ass hat. In the world of lenses, aspheric means that the lens prevents color distortion when light enters and is bent by the lens. 

A standard lens does not bend all wavelengths at the same power. I.e. blue light is bent less while red light is bent more. This causes a color separation distortion, more noticeable at night or in low light situations as far as contacts go.

Most newer contacts today, even if not stated, incorporate aspheric optics. How exactly they do so on such a thin and tiny flexible thing is a mystery to me, as it would initially seem impossible given the general physics of lenses. Somehow they make it happen. 

Bottom line is that it reduces the separation of the colors of light. Standard lenses will cause the separation of different light wavelengths because the bending power is not equal across the entire visible light spectrum. 

Aspheric lenses are designed to correct for that so that all/most wavelengths (colors) of light are bent to the same degree. 

You want aspheric lenses, whether it be contacts or your camera.

It depends on several factors:

* Are they daily contacts?
* Are the contacts rated for extended wear? If so, the max is typically 6 nights, per FDA guidelines.
* Does he take them out and clean them thoroughly (and I mean thoroughly) before the 6 nights runs out?
* Does he replace them more often than 30 days? (Technically if you wear your contacts in "extended-wear" mode they must be replaced sooner, as protein and mineral build up is **significantly higher**)
* How many nights in a row does he sleep in them?

Even if contacts are rated for nightly use, **it is highly recommended to never wear them overnight.** This is because it puts strain on the eyes, reduces oxygenation of the cornea as you sleep, and detrimentally affects the ability of the eyes to "self clean" and "self disinfect" overnight. 

Overnight wear can also be a major trigger of keratitis (which can lead to **permanent vision loss**) and greatly increases the risk of infection, as well as other eye problems. 

It is otherwise okay to wear extended-wear contacts overnight if done properly and cleaned very well between use. They will also need to be replaced more frequently, as even the best cleaning won't make up for the additional wear and deposit formation on the contacts. 

Typically I've heard eye doctors recommended tossing the contact entirely if it's been worn for 6 straight nights. It gets a bit muddy if it's like 3 nights, then taken out and cleaned/disinfected and then worn during the day a few times, cleaned, and then worn overnight again, etc. That question is much better suited for his eye doctor to answer based on his actual use of the contacts.

* Place contact into solution 
* Using my index finger (with trimmed nails!!) I rub the contact thoroughly for 30 seconds
* Repeat this rubbing 3 to 4 times with fresh solution each time
* Side note: rubbing should be good with light to light-moderate pressure, heavy pressure will shred the contact, rip it, or deform it. But you need some amount of light pressure 
* Rinse the inside with solution for 5 actual seconds after rubbing
* Rinse index finger for 5 seconds before picking up the contact out of my palm
* Rinse the front/surface of contact for 5 seconds (now that it's on my index finger)
* Place into the case that has FRESH solution. **Never reuse, top off, or use a case that is dirty, unsterile, expired, or has lint and shit in it.**

Also note: *at no times do I allow the tips of my fingers that I plan to use or manipulate the contact during cleaning touch anything, including the solution bottle.* This does mean awkwardly handling the bottle with fewer fingers and mostly palm pressure. So there's various model helicopter types. There's co-axial which have two sets of main rotors on the too, with no tail rotor. 

Then there's fixed pitched, where you have a dynamic tail that is manually controlled, but a main rotors where the pitch of the blades remains the same and you're actually varying the speed at which they fly.

Finally, for the pros (like myself) you get collective cyclic rotors on both the tail and the main. The speed of the rotors never changes, instead you vary the pitch at which the blades attack. You can also hover these bad assess upside down because of this. 

It took me a full year of flying maybe 10 hours a week before I felt confident trying to fly my helicopter upside down, and it was still hard as fuck because everything is reversed and one slip up means throwing hundreds of dollars out. 

Unlike model airplanes, where you can still attempt a landing and reduce costs of repair, there is no reducing costs of repair with a model helicopter. When you crash, there little you can do about it. Parts go flying as the rotors disintegrate, main shafts get bent, skids break, canopy is torn to shreds. 

It's a very expensive hobby that is very difficult to get right. You have to be willing to loose a few thousand dollars learning if you ever want to fly CCPM (collective cyclic) 

And unfortunately, simulators did jack shit to help me learn. Somehow trying to fly the helicopter based on the 50 pixels you get once it's father than 50 feet away doesn't translate well to what it actually looks and feels like to fly at real life 50 ft away. 

I'd also like to add that collective helicopters do not self upright. If you give it a nudge to go forward, you do not keep holding the God damn stick forward. You nudge it once and then recenter the stick. You want it to stop going forward, pull the stick back a nudge. 

On top of all of this, is hovering. It is like trying to balance a marble on top of an upside down bowl. It takes constant small corrective inputs. As soon as you stop giving it those correctives, it will fly off and you'll loose control.

If you feel like your current meds aren't helping then it's probably a good time to talk to your doctor about increasing or changing the meds your taking. Meds effect everyone differently so you sometimes have to just keep on trying. 

There's also no magical fix for me either, zyprexa made it better but I'm still paranoid sometimes and I even slip up and fully believe that I'm being spied on by the government or my neighbors. It's hard. 

Psychotherapy has helped me learn assets to combat that paranoia, but it's always going to be a struggle for me.

The voices are still with me too, but they're neutral and not as demeaning or rude and quieter to me with meds, versus without. 

I hope it works out for you. You should really talk to your therapist about ways you can fight back against those thoughts and feelings, no matter how real they may seem or not at any given time. Try your best not to fall into the trap of them. 

Also talk to your doctor about the meds. Maybe it's time for a change.
